entry.title: CFL-aware edge design for graph neural solvers of hyperbolic transport
entry.summary: Hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) transport information at finite speed along characteristics, often producing shocks and discontinuities that are challenging to capture numerically. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer learned update rules, but neighbor aggregation alone does not tell a GNN how far information must travel and along which edge. As a result, when a GNN model takes a time step larger than what was used in training, shock fronts smear and oscillations grow. In this work, we ask whether making the scale of transport explicit as an edge-local Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) signal can enhance GNNs' ability to model hyperbolic PDEs. Holding the architecture fixed, we vary only the information given to each edge, from a raw edge form to forms that progressively expose the edge-local transport interaction through direction, length, and wave speed. Because all of these are computed from the same ingredients, what changes is not the amount of information but its form. The results show a consistent pattern, in which feature count is not the limiting factor, and appending CFL directly to a raw edge form produces almost no benefit. The CFL conditioning proves most effective when the edge information already exposes the transport interaction, reducing final-step error by 10.4-14.4%, and the improvement widens as the step size grows larger. Notably, this improvement arises not from smearing the solution but from suppressing oscillations near shocks. These results point to a specific design principle that CFL conditioning is most effective when the edge representation already separates the direction of interaction from spatial scale, so that the CFL value has a well-defined quantity to modulate.

entry.title: Six-Degree-of-Freedom Rotor-Load Cross-Spectral Density from Rotor-Plane Turbulence Cross-Spectra
entry.summary: A frequency-domain response analysis of a wind turbine rotor requires the complete hub-load spectrum, but the customary scalar thrust and torque spectra retain neither the four in-plane components nor the coupling between them. This paper derives the full six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) rotor-load cross-spectral-density (CSD) matrix from the IEC Kaimal turbulence model. By decoupling the spatial order of inflow coherence from the temporal Doppler shift, the formulation introduces a two-index rotational-sampling kernel. Rotor symmetry and azimuthal averaging constrain the observed Doppler carrier strictly to blade-passing harmonics $pBf_{\mathrm{rot}}$, while the azimuthal aerodynamic transfer shifts the spatial coherence order to $pB+s$. A convergence study of the retained azimuthal order $s$ shows that $\lvert s\rvert\le4$ suffices, the assembled CSD then deviating from the full-band result by less than $10^{-5}$ in relative norm. The formulation is compared with OpenFAST simulations of a rigid floating wind turbine over nine wind speeds: the six auto-spectral densities agree closely below 1~Hz, and the present theory over-predicts the spectra near the 6P and 9P rotational harmonics.

entry.title: Elasto-Plastocapillarity: Surface-Tension-Driven Flows of Yield-Stress Fluids
entry.summary: In this perspective article, we introduce elasto-plastocapillarity: surface-tension-driven free-surface flows of yield-stress fluids in which capillary stresses compete with yielding and elastic relaxation. We frame the relevant parameter space, and highlight representative problems (drops, bubbles, jets/filaments, thin films, and porous media) that are central to applications ranging from additive manufacturing and coatings to biological flows. We then outline a set of timely open challenges, including surface-tension measurements, breakdown of scale separation near the microstructures, coupled bulk-interface flow experimental diagnosis, interfacial rheology and surface stresses, history dependence, constitutive models and boundary conditions, reduced theoretical models, and the emerging opportunity provided by artificial intelligence and microgravity; aimed at guiding future experiments, theory, and computation.

entry.title: Predicting the onset of airfoil stall in transitional and turbulent flows with a pressure-gradient-based separation model for RANS simulations
entry.summary: We propose an improved version of the $k$-$ω$ shear-stress transport Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes model that supersedes our prior work (Griffin et al. 2024 J. Turb.) with an updated pressure-gradient sensor that generalizes well across geometries and to laminar, transitional, and turbulent flows alike. The model is based on a composite pressure gradient criterion that uses the solution of an intermittency transport equation to synthesize the separation criteria of the Falkner-Skan theory for laminar flows and the continuously critical theory for turbulent flows. The proposed model is applied to various airfoils including the thick airfoils representative of wind turbine applications (DU00-w-212, S809 and S814) and thinner airfoils used in aerospace applications [NACA23012 and NLF(1)-0416]. For all airfoils, the proposed model is found to preserve or improve the predictions of the baseline model for both fully turbulent and transitional airfoils as demonstrated with results for the lift and drag coefficients. The model is also found to improve the prediction of separation on the NREL Phase VI rotor in a preliminary study, suggesting that the model will generalize to other complex three-dimensional flows.

entry.title: Trapped sausage modes in magnetic pores: existence criteria and viscous damping
entry.summary: The conditions governing the existence and evolution of trapped sausage waves in photospheric magnetic pores are investigated, with particular emphasis on the limitations of analytical cut-off criteria and the role of viscous dissipation. A pore is modelled as a cylindrical magnetic flux tube with smoothly varying radial profiles of magnetic field and density, subject to the constraint that its temperature is lower than that of the surrounding atmosphere. For finite plasma-$β$, the linearised equations governing sausage-mode perturbations are derived, and an initial-value problem is solved numerically to obtain the full spatio-temporal evolution of the waves. The applicability of the analytical cut-off relation derived for a flux tube with step-function equilibrium profiles is examined, revealing that its predictions depend on the equilibrium parameters. The simulations reveal distinct wave behaviours across different parameter regimes, including the simultaneous excitation of trapped fast and slow sausage waves for a representative photospheric parameter set. Viscous damping is further investigated through the temporal evolution of the wave energy. Energy dissipation increases with decreasing viscous Reynolds number, increasing longitudinal wavenumber, and increasing radial magnetic-field contrast. These trends are consistent with enhanced viscous damping associated with increasingly fine spatial gradients generated through phase mixing. The findings highlight the importance of radial equilibrium structure in assessing sausage-wave trapping and demonstrate the sensitivity of wave-energy dissipation to the physical parameters of photospheric magnetic pores.

entry.title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes
entry.summary: Thermal-fluid field distributions underpin the analysis and operation of energy infrastructure, from nuclear-reactor cooling channels to industrial heat exchangers, but resolving these distributions through computational fluid dynamics requires prohibitively large simulation ensembles. Their complex geometries also demand unstructured meshes that are poorly accommodated by generative models developed for regular grids. Here we introduce FlowMesh, a generative framework that combines permutation-invariant mesh encoding with deterministic latent flow matching and an l1 penalty on the learned transport velocity. FlowMesh generates full-field realizations directly on fixed unstructured meshes without auxiliary grid interpolation or a stochastic denoising chain. Across lid-driven-cavity, pressurized-water-reactor subchannel and heat-exchanger datasets, evaluated over six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieves macro-averaged probability-density-function coverage of 91.7%-97.0%, exceeding an architecture-controlled latent diffusion model by $11.6$--$45.4$ percentage points. Latent-velocity regularization increases coverage by $3.8$ percentage points for reactor flows and 1.1 points for heat-exchanger flows, while reducing temperature-field Kullback--Leibler divergence by 1.7-2.4-fold. Each full-field realization requires 1.23 \pm 0.15 s, providing a 585--1902-fold wall-clock acceleration over computational fluid dynamics. FlowMesh therefore makes large-scale generative characterization of thermal-fluid states computationally feasible, providing a foundation for data-driven analysis and digital-twin development in fixed-geometry energy systems.

entry.title: Ideal interaction dynamics of defects and background fields in condensed matter
entry.summary: While defect dynamics in condensed matter systems is widely studied and several methods are available to track the defect position over time, the formulation of dynamical models for the coupled evolution of both defect and background field quantities seems to be more challenging. Yet, the overall behavior of a system containing moving defects is strongly influenced by this defect-field interaction. Here, we propose a modeling framework for the conservative coupled evolution of the defect density and the background fields upon focusing on two relevant cases of study: the Gross-Pitaevskii theory of quantum fluids and the Ericksen-Leslie model of nematic liquid crystals. To achieve the coupled evolution, we combine the Euler-Poincaré variational setting of continuum dynamics with the gauge theory of topological defects. While the latter allows us to overcome certain ambiguities in definition of the defect density, the Euler-Poincaré method provides a unified modeling approach in the absence of defect reconnection.

entry.title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
entry.summary: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

entry.title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
entry.summary: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

entry.title: Chaos Made Visible: Active particles trace Lorenz-like attractors in physical space
entry.summary: Chaotic attractors are typically visualized in an abstract phase space. Here we show that an orientable active particle moving through a steady, two-dimensional, multivortex flow can trace a Lorenz-like chaotic attractor in its real space trajectory. Despite the flow being strictly time independent, coupling between particle position and orientation creates a three-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system. For suitable particle shape and swimming speed, the trajectory organizes into a striking two-lobed geometry reminiscent of the classical Lorenz attractor. A structured first return map, positive largest Lyapunov exponent, and a broadband power spectrum establish that the underlying motion is chaotic. Varying the swimming speed reveals a rich sequence of dynamical regimes as self-propulsion breaks streamline confinement and reorganizes the particle motion. Our results demonstrate how an internal orientational degree of freedom can make chaotic dynamics directly visible in physical space, allowing a single active particle to trace a chaotic attractor as it moves through an otherwise steady flow.

entry.title: When does boundary-condition uncertainty outweigh thermal and vegetation effects in street canyon flow? A global sensitivity analysis of input uncertainty
entry.summary: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is increasingly used to resolve wind, heat, and pollution patterns in cities with high fidelity but high computational cost. Thermal effects and vegetation are often neglected despite being important drivers, yet their influence may be masked by variability from other uncertain inputs. This work determines how precisely model parameters and boundary conditions must be known for these effects to govern output uncertainty in the velocity, temperature, and concentration fields of a two-dimensional street canyon. A global Sobol analysis of 24 parameters is made tractable by a surrogate trained on Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations, combining principal component analysis (PCA) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Two ventilation regimes assess the variance due to thermal and vegetation parameters as uncertainty in all other inputs is progressively reduced. At typical uncertainty levels, turbulence closure constants and inflow turbulence profiles govern variability in all three fields in both regimes. Under weak ventilation, solar forcing becomes the main source of temperature variability once the remaining uncertainties are halved, and of concentration variance once they are reduced to a quarter (about $\pm11\%$ for the dominant closure constant and $\pm12\%$ for the emission rate). In contrast, vegetation contributes significantly at typical uncertainty levels. Under strong ventilation, however, the canopy never overtakes the closure constants, even when the dominant one is known to $\pm5\%$. Spatially, both effects peak at road level and along canyon walls, which influence outdoor exposure and indoor infiltration, suggesting that high-resolution exposure studies should account for them.

entry.title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
entry.summary: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

entry.title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget
entry.summary: The fidelity of direct numerical simulation now outpaces the storage and data-movement capacity available for the resulting fields. We present an open, distributed, GPU-accelerated low-rank compression framework for large turbulent flow databases. We assess it using two direct numerical simulations of a controlled diffusion compressor cascade under laminar and turbulent inflow conditions. Compression is formulated using a correlation operator over space and time, which is two orders of magnitude larger than that of snapshot POD. Its dominant range is extracted with a randomized range finder based on communication-avoiding hierarchical QR. The compressed databases are evaluated through a hierarchy of increasingly strict diagnostics, from instantaneous reconstruction and second-order statistics to the modal turbulent kinetic energy budget and its nonlinear interscale transfer. The budget terms are far more sensitive to compression than fieldwise or one-point errors. They remain accurate at conservative compression and degrade sharply once the retained energy is relaxed. The near-wall dissipation and the interscale transfer degrade the most and set the admissible compression level. An aggressive reduction preserves every one-point statistic to within a few per cent while corrupting both by an order of magnitude more. The dissipation error is confined to the viscous sublayer and grows with the development of the boundary layer. It is carried by the high-order modes. For both inflows, the linear budget terms scale with the discarded energy to the power $0.8$ and the triadic transfer to a power above one.
entry.arxiv:comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to Computers & Fluids

entry.title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
entry.summary: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

entry.title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
entry.summary: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

entry.title: Heat vortices and the vorticity triplet in kinetic phonon transport: a fluid-dynamical perspective
entry.summary: From a novel fluid-dynamical perspective, the present study investigates the heat-current vortices and heat vorticity in heat conduction process of solid materials. The heat vorticity $\bmω$, defined as the curl of the heat-flux field, is decomposed into the orbital-rotation $\bm{R}$ and spin $\bm{S}$, which collectively constitute the heat-vorticity triplet $(\bm{R},\bm{S},\bmω)$, extending beyond the existing single-vorticity research paradigm. As an illustrative example, kinetic phonon transport in a 2D porous solid structure is examined based on the numerical solutions of the Peierls-Boltzmann equation under the Callway dual-relaxation-time approximation. The physical characteristics of heat vortices and the vorticity triplet patterns are analyzed across different kinetic regimes in the phase diagram of the normal (N) and resistive (R) scattering processes.... In the hydrodynamic limit, the boundary generation mechanism of heat vorticity is further elucidated based on the Guyer-Krumhansl (G-K) equation generated from the truncated Chapman-Enskog (C-E) expansion. The boundary heat vorticity flux (BHVF) is proposed as a new concept for describing the local rate at which heat vorticity is generated at the boundary of a solid material. The general expression for the BHVF is rigorously derived for phonon hydrodynamics, and for the 2D steady hydrodynamic phonon transport case, we find that the BHVF is solely attributed to the tangential component of the net heat flux deviating from the classical Fourier heat flux. Furthermore, we show that the total vorticity contained in a control volume arises from the spatiotemporal accumulation of the BHVF, weighted by the memory kernel arising from the R scattering. The proposed theory and findings herein could be valuable for understanding the diverse vortical-flow phenomena in condensed matter systems.

entry.title: IMRFit: Interactive Simulation and Constitutive-Model Fitting for Inertial Microcavitation Rheometry
entry.summary: Inertial microcavitation rheometry (IMR) characterizes the high-rate mechanical response of soft materials from the rapid expansion and collapse of a microscopic bubble. In a typical IMR experiment, high-speed imaging provides the bubble radius as a function of time, R(t), and material parameters are identified by comparing the measured response with simulations that couple bubble dynamics to a constitutive description of the surrounding medium. This inverse analysis requires repeated forward simulations and careful control of experimental inputs, material parameters, and fitting settings. IMRFit is an open-source Python desktop application that brings these steps into an interactive environment for forward simulation, parameter identification, and constitutive-model comparison. Users can import experimental radius-time data, select a bubble-dynamics formulation and constitutive model, inspect simulated responses, fit material parameters, and organize batch fitting and parameter-sweep jobs. IMRFit includes Neo-Hookean Kelvin-Voigt and generalized Maxwell-Ogden-based models, among other constitutive options, and supports additional models through JSON descriptors and Python solver entry points. It also integrates fitting-window selection, visualization, and data export into a single workflow.

entry.title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier-Stokes turbulence
entry.summary: Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of the deterministic Navier-Stokes (NS) equations is widely used to provide benchmark solutions of turbulent flow, but its accuracy and reliability have not been rigorously inspected from a mathematical viewpoint. Here we prove a spatial symmetry invariance theorem (SSIT) of three-dimensional NS equations whereby an exact solution of deterministic NS equations under periodic boundary conditions maintains the same spatial symmetry as its symmetric initial flow, forever. SSIT provides an absolute benchmark test for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). It is shown herein that traditional DNS of NS turbulence quickly violates SSIT, revealing that the spatiotemporal trajectory of NS turbulence predicted by DNS soon becomes badly polluted by numerical noise. Importantly, it is found that even the statistical results of DNS might be unstable, i.e., exhibit sensitivity dependence on the initial flow conditions. In other words, the loss of spatial symmetry in traditional DNS of NS turbulence is not a physical instability but instead a numerical artifact caused by the chaotic nature of the flow. Using the SSIT, it is straightforward to deduce several key properties of NS turbulence, including `ultra-chaos', the so-called `noise-expansion cascade', `permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions', and so on. Note that permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions suggests that NS turbulence governed by deterministic NS equations subject to symmetric initial flow should have no `mixing', corresponding to non-ergodicity, although ergodicity is one of the most fundamental assumptions of turbulence theory.

entry.title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels
entry.summary: In a zero-gravity cylindrical container, a meniscus can span a square or equilateral-triangular cross-section only at contact angles at or above the respective Concus-Finn critical angles of 45 degrees and 60 degrees. We study strong-form physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across these thresholds under fixed collocation and optimization budgets. Classical capillary flux balance yields a lower bound on the combined interior and wall residual loss for arbitrary positive sampling densities. In the tested nonexistence regime, several degrees below the critical angles, independently evaluated network losses are 1.6-1.9 times this bound. A polynomial least-squares comparison supports the same geometric interpretation. The PINNs still return smooth graphs with finite axial extent, even though the prescribed equilibrium problem has no spanning graph solution. Their small interior residuals coexist with wall-flux deficits near corners, where adjoining contact-angle conditions demand more flux than a finite-slope graph can supply. Residuals vary on both sides of the critical angle, while the bound tends uniformly to zero at threshold for fixed wall weight. These results give a geometric scale for interpreting the computed loss and locate the incompatibility that a small interior residual can conceal.
entry.arxiv:comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Includes the main text and complete Supplementary Material

entry.title: Anchored HLLD: A Riemann solver for a hypoelastic diffuse-interface model of compressible fluid-solid interaction
entry.summary: We present an HLLD Riemann solver for a multicomponent hypoelastic diffuse-interface model of compressible fluid-solid interaction, with no separately computed interface and a deviatoric stress advanced by an objective hypoelastic rate law outside conservation-law form. The difficulty specific to this model is that the stress evolution is nonconservative and, unlike the familiar volume-fraction terms of Kapila-type models, cannot be left outside the Riemann solve once the shear waves are resolved. The shear coefficient $ρ(G+τ_{xx})$ sets the impedance of the resolved shear waves and so belongs to their eigenstructure. Anchored HLLD carries it inside the solve by evaluating the HLLD fan twice at each face, anchored in turn to each adjacent cell-centered state, with every cell advancing from the flux anchored to its own state. HLL, HLLC, and anchored HLLD form a three-tier hierarchy of increasing wave resolution in one framework. We prove local structural properties: consistency at the reconstruction order, exact species-mass conservation, and tangential-momentum and energy drift vanishing under refinement at the reconstruction's face-jump order on smooth fields, with one-dimensional tests illustrating these structural properties and demonstrating first-order drift convergence on discontinuous fields. Across one-dimensional tests and two-dimensional production simulations in the open-source solver MFC, anchored HLLD resolves both the material contact and the shear waves, HLLC the contact alone, and HLL neither sharply. Where refinement studies are shown, anchored HLLD converges toward exact or semi-analytic solutions. A three-dimensional shock-ellipsoid interaction demonstrates the solver with all six stress components active.

entry.title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
entry.summary: Conventional particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) has been the standard diagnostic tool for studying fluid and granular flows. However, in dense granular systems, the average distance moved by particles between frames can approach or exceed inter-particle spacing, demanding ultra-high frame rates. Furthermore, neighbouring particles may move together, and common velocity-based prediction fails after energetic collisions. Existing methods struggle to track granular particles without losing identities or swapping. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV), a training-free multi-pass method leveraging multicoloured particles to achieve enhanced tracking. CBTV first matches constellations of neighbouring coloured particles as single units, guided by a cross-correlation motion prior, and only then assigns the remaining particles individually. We compare it with 12 baseline tracker configurations, from classical linkers to graph-neural-network and transformer models, on 59 cases from 15 simulated discrete-element granular flows with exact ground truth (0.006-9 diameters/frame). CBTV matches or exceeds every tracker tested on an impulsive collision at every displacement. Its advantage lies in dense flows in which particles move between about half and twice their spacing per frame, where links between frames are ambiguous. On agitated shear flow, a colour relaxation tracker, which also uses neighbour context, matches or narrowly exceeds CBTV. Where links are unambiguous, CBTV is close to the best tracker, and beyond about two to three particle diameters per frame, the range of its motion prior, trackers that compensate for bulk motion are more accurate. For experimentalists, dense granular flows of coloured particles can be tracked at displacements per frame where trackers without neighbour context lose identities, easing the demand for ultra-high frame rates without training data.

entry.title: High-order Simulation of Nearly Hydrostatic Atmospheric Flows
entry.summary: Accurate simulation of atmospheric flows is challenging. Low-Mach-number dynamics often need to be resolved in the presence of a dominant, nearly hydrostatic background state. Conventional upwind numerical fluxes can introduce excessive acoustic-speed-based dissipation in the low-Mach regime. Discretization errors in the balance law can also generate spurious motion. This work investigates these two issues within a high-order Direct Flux Reconstruction (DFR) framework coupled with a third-order exponential time integrator for the 3D compressible Euler equations with gravity. Low-Mach-number accuracy is addressed using a modified AUSM$^+$-up flux, denoted AUSM$^+$-upH. Preservation of the background equilibrium is improved through a deviation-based formulation. The resulting approach is assessed using a hierarchy of idealized atmospheric test cases. The results show that AUSM$^+$-upH preserves low-Mach flow structures more effectively than the more dissipative Rusanov flux. However, reduced numerical dissipation also makes AUSM$^+$-upH more sensitive to residual errors in the discrete hydrostatic balance. The deviation formulation substantially suppresses these errors by several orders of magnitude, with the strongest improvement observed for flows over orography. Overall, AUSM$^+$-upH exhibits greater robustness when combined with the deviation formulation across the atmospheric test cases considered.

entry.title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows
entry.summary: Data-driven reduced-order modelling (ROM) of turbulent flows is based on an efficient and physical low-dimensional representation of the flow process. Such a dimension reduction can be achieved using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) or non-linear autoencoders. Capturing the inherent non-linearities in turbulent flows offers the potential for improved compression rates. This work proposes the local tangent residual (LTR) as an a priori estimate of the potential benefit of non-linear dimension reduction for a given dataset. The LTR is based on the local geometry of the data points, requiring neither prior model training nor the definition of a threshold parameter. For all datasets investigated in this work, namely, two vortex street cases and the turbulent wake flow of a wind turbine, the dominant trends in autoencoder compression performance are reproduced by the proposed LTR. The results are further contextualised through the decoder linearisation error (DLE). The DLE quantifies the non-linearity of the trained decoder by comparing it to a linearised surrogate model, which enables physical interpretability of the non-linearities. Together, a large non-linear compression potential in the turbulent flow, as quantified by the LTR, is corroborated by a large DLE, i.e., a pronounced non-linearity captured in the trained autoencoder. The LTR thus enables practitioners in turbulent flow modelling to determine a priori whether non-linear compression is worthwhile, avoiding the substantial computational cost of autoencoder architecture search and hyperparameter tuning in cases where POD already suffices.

entry.title: Strongly non-linear continuous model for wave propagation in 2D granular media: derivation and hyperbolicity analysis
entry.summary: In this work, we develop a nonlinear continuum model for wave propagation in two-dimensional granular materials, building on key ideas from Nesterenko's work. Starting from the Hertzian contact law and neglecting contact friction, we derive an effective continuum description through homogenization, assuming spherical, monodisperse grains, local periodicity, and the Cauchy--Born hypothesis. The resulting strain-gradient model depends on both the first and second gradients of the displacement field. We analyse the hyperbolicity of the leading-order system through its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, establishing conditions for hyperbolicity within a restricted deformation domain. The model is solved using an explicit finite-volume method to investigate gravitational settling and wave propagation. We derive analytical expressions for the longitudinal and transverse wave speeds and highlight their dependence on depth. Finally, the predictions of the continuum model are compared with existing discrete-element simulations. This formulation allows several extensions, including more complex packing geometries, contact laws, and large-deformation regimes in which the contact network can evolve.

entry.title: A novel machine learning framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition for turbine wake flow predictions in natural waterways
entry.summary: We developed a machine learning (ML) surrogate trained on instantaneous large eddy simulation (LES) data filtered using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to predict mean flow fields in natural rivers with complex geometries. The surrogate enables efficient prediction of mean flow fields downstream of marine hydrokinetic (MHK) turbine arrays at a fraction of the computational cost of high fidelity simulations, facilitating turbine layout optimization in natural waterways where bathymetry, turbulence, and turbine interactions influence the available energy resource. We demonstrate the capabilities of the model at a real world tidal river site under ebb tide conditions. Complex bed bathymetry and planform geometry generate substantial background turbulence that can obscure turbine wake signatures. POD is employed to extract relevant flow structures, improving the ability of the ML model to learn wake dynamics. First, LES is performed at the tidal site to generate training data. POD is then applied to decompose the instantaneous LES fields into spatial modes. Selected modes are used to train a three dimensional convolutional encoder decoder network to predict time averaged velocity fields. This selective filtering reduces the influence of dominant background fluctuations while preserving information relevant to turbine wakes. At equivalent network size and training cost, the POD filtered surrogate reduces the mean squared error by three orders of magnitude compared with the same network trained on unfiltered LES data.

entry.title: Modulation theory of Y- and X-wave Kadomtsev--Petviashvili solitons
entry.summary: The evolution of long wavelength perturbations of traveling wave 2-soliton solutions of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili II (KP) equation are investigated using modulation theory. An initial-boundary value problem for a system of hyperbolic conservation laws is formulated for amplitude and slope perturbations to soliton legs of the resonant (Y-shaped) and X-shaped KP traveling wave solutions. The vertex where individuated soliton legs coalesce is modeled as a moving free boundary where information between the soliton legs can pass. The linearized hyperbolic system is proven to be well-posed under suitable initial conditions and is solved exactly. In the case of the resonant Y-shaped soliton, all admissible simple (rarefaction) waves of the nonlinear system are characterized. Specific perturbations of Y-waves can lead to the dimensionality of the modulated solution changing, corresponding to a physical geometric change to the multi-soliton pattern. Spontaneous leg deletion and leg creation can occur. The conditions under which the Y-wave modulation system can experience gradient catastrophe are given. Gradient catastrophe is regularized by the formation of a new leg, with an augmented modulation system proposed to describe the growth of the new leg. On the other hand, the X-wave system can be reduced to two independent line soliton modulation systems. These findings reinforce the prevalence and generality of resonant Y-shaped vertices in the KP II system and applications.The theoretical modulation predictions are supported by direct numerical simulations of KP II, which show good agreement with the analysis.

entry.title: Tandem jets in crossflow: the enclosed-recirculation momentum exchange and the unsteady shear-layer dynamics
entry.summary: Twin tandem jets in crossflow are examined by 40\ kHz time-resolved particle image velocimetry (PIV) over nine spacing--velocity-ratio conditions ($L=2d$--$4d$, $r\approx3$--7; 68 twin cases, 11 single-jet records). The front jet is diluted: its trajectory lies below the single-jet reference, with a near-field segment up to 40\% shorter, and its velocity ratio falls to an effective value $r_{\mathrm{eff}}<r$, while the shielded rear jet rises above the reference. This paper identifies the carrier of that dilution and the unsteady dynamics that sustains it. The rear-jet blockage closes a gap recirculation whose reversed flow puts the two gap-side layers in the counter-current shear-layer configuration, the classical route to enhanced entrainment. The measured Reynolds stress and Prandtl mixing length show that the absolute exchange is nearly independent of the velocity ratio and exceeds the single-jet leeward zone like-for-like by up to $1.5\times$ (zone peak, across conditions) and $2.8\times$ (area-integrated) at $r\approx7$. The gain comes from an enlarged mixing scale rather than from a steeper shear, and the front-jet near-field shortening follows the absolute exchange transport rather than the twin/single enhancement ratio. The turbulent term exceeds the pressure term in eight of the nine conditions, and the flux budget reads the dilution as a limited mass addition plus a momentum loss to the crossflow; the evidence remains observational. The gap-side layers remain convectively unstable---DMD and SPOD find no growing mode within the resolvable band and record length---so the exchange is carried by convecting vortex trains rather than by a self-excited global mode.

entry.title: Anisotropic spin hydrodynamics in a magnetized medium: entropy-current formulation and minimal linear modes
entry.summary: We formulate anisotropic relativistic spin hydrodynamics in a parity-even magnetized medium using an Israel--Stewart entropy-current construction. Treating the magnetic field at leading order in the gradient expansion reduces the rotational symmetry to $SO(2)$ and separates spin susceptibilities and dissipative transport into longitudinal, transverse, and mixed channels. A restricted quadratic entropy current yields transient equations for the retained dissipative stresses and spin fluxes. We analyze a minimal linear closure around an unpolarized homogeneous equilibrium, retaining dynamical magnetic-flux perturbations but no explicit spin-magnetization coupling; spin and magnetic fluctuations mix through the fluid variables. Infrared coefficient equations and ultraviolet characteristic expansions organize the magnetosonic and Alfvén-like spectra together with spectator spin-flux poles. The first-order truncation exhibits unstable boost-sector poles and superlinear large-wave-number branches, interpreted as diagnostics of the truncated equations rather than microscopic dispersion predictions. For the baseline parameters, finite relaxation times yield asymptotically linear propagation branches and finite relaxation poles, with no growing modes found on the sampled grid. The characteristic speeds depend nonmonotonically on spin transport and provide necessary light-cone diagnostics, without establishing general stability or strong hyperbolicity.

entry.title: A second-order linear decoupled scheme with a relaxed zero-energy variable for Rayleigh-Bénard convection
entry.summary: We construct a second-order, linear, and fully decoupled scheme for Rayleigh--Bénard convection between Navier-slip walls. The nonlinear terms are treated explicitly and multiplied by a scalar with exact value $1$ and no energy contributed to the continuous problem. As a result, each BDF2 step, with a rotational pressure correction, solves only constant-coefficient linear problems. For the time discretization, we prove that, for any time-step, the energy decays when the walls have equal temperatures, under a condition on the thermal weight, and the energy is bounded on finite time intervals when heated from below. Relaxing the scalar towards $1$ preserves both estimates. Energy stability does not control the accuracy of the scalar; the velocity and temperature fields are computed with its unrelaxed value, whose deviation from $1$ scales like $(E/C)(δt/τ)^3$ for kinetic energy $E$, time-scale $τ$ of the flow, and weight $C$ of the scalar equation. In our tests, choosing $C$ comparable to $E$ keeps this deviation small and doubles the largest time-step for which steady rolls are reproduced to a relative difference of $10^{-8}$. With Taylor--Hood elements, we observe second-order convergence in time, recover the critical Rayleigh numbers, and match published Nusselt numbers to within $0.5\%$. A three-dimensional implementation passes corresponding validation tests.

entry.title: A Universal Constitutive Relation for Static Droplet Retention
entry.summary: Under applied forcing, static droplet retention is accompanied by contact angle asymmetry, with unequal apparent contact angles on opposite sides. Yet, the relation between the asymmetry and forcing lacks a common constitutive basis. Here, we show that the asymmetry emerges from minimizing the forcing-dependent free energy. The response of the asymmetry to forcing defines a susceptibility whose zero-forcing value yields a universal constitutive relation between the asymmetry and forcing. The constitutive relation is quantitatively validated across liquids, volumes, and forcing levels.

entry.title: Extracting target-related flow structures using a time-lagged cross-correlation ranking criterion
entry.summary: Structures with large global contributions to a flow field are not necessarily those that are most closely associated with a specified engineering observable. We propose a time-lagged cross-correlation (TCC) ranking criterion to extract target-related dynamical structures from a fixed modal expansion while preserving existing spatial modes and temporal coefficients. The criterion ranks mode groups by the mean squared norm of cross-responses between their flow contributions and the observable over a lag window. It is tested separately using dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). TCC-DMD analysis shows that TCC recovers three low-contribution target structures from a dominant background in a synthetic flow. The reconstruction error for the target subfield is 2.15\%. In the cylinder wake, different force observables select structures associated with the vortex-shedding fundamental, slow drag variations, and the second harmonic. In the cavity case, selected modes connect two main frequency bands of the target observable to distinct spatial amplitude and phase distributions. TCC-POD analysis shows that the criterion minimises the weighted truncation error of the correlation operator among equally sized subsets of the fixed orthogonal basis. A comparison with canonical correlation decomposition further reveals differences between fixed-direction selection and correlation-based basis construction in the spatial structure and retention of flow information. Lag aggregation can improve structure identification when zero-lag association is insufficient. The gains depend on the cross-response distribution and window selection. TCC separates target-related ranking from mode-set construction, enabling comparison of spatial structures associated with different observables within the same modal expansion.

entry.title: Quartz Crystal Microbalance impedance of discrete adsorbates with lubricated contact
entry.summary: We present a thorough theoretical investigation of the shear force exerted on a horizontal plate undergoing fast (MHz range) longitudinal oscillations in presence of a spherical particle suspended in the liquid at close proximity to the plate. This hydrodynamic problem is relevant toward the analysis of frequency response (i.e., complex impedance) of Quartz Crystal Microbalance (QCM) to discrete (particulate) adsorbates. For low areal density of adsorbates, the contributions of individual particles remain additive, rendering the theory applicable towards quantitative interpretation of the experimental measurements. For adsorbates much smaller than the viscous penetration depth, the closed-form analytical expressions for the complex impedance were derived for particles of arbitrary density, assuming a lubricated contact (i.e., non-localized adsorption). The theoretical predictions were shown to be in an excellent agreement with accurate Finite Element numerical computations. The validity of the theoretical approach was confirmed by QCM measurements conducted for polystyrene nanoparticles in a broad range of sizes, from 32 nm to 510 nm, adsorbing onto gold/silica sensor upon varying the oscillation frequency.

entry.title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method
entry.summary: Regularized lattice Boltzmann methods improve numerical stability by projecting the nonequilibrium distribution onto its hydrodynamic second-order Hermite sector and filtering the remaining kinetic modes. We introduce a separate relaxation time for the complete complementary kinetic subspace. The resulting extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method (E-RLBM) interpolates continuously between the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and regularized collision operators while retaining a two-rate implementation. A Chapman-Enskog expansion shows that the isothermal Navier-Stokes equations are recovered with kinematic viscosity $ν=c_s^2(τ-Δt/2)$, independently of the kinetic relaxation time $τ_{\rm nh}$, whereas $τ_{\rm nh}$ changes higher-order truncation errors. For linear transverse shear, its first effect is a fourth-derivative term whose coefficient depends on the direction of propagation relative to the lattice. This fourth-order coefficient is affine in $τ_{\rm nh}$. For linear shear on D2Q9 and $τ_{\rm nh}$ between $τ$ and $Δt$, it lies between the corresponding BGK and RLBM values in every propagation direction. Stability maps for the decaying Taylor-Green vortex and flow past a rectangular obstacle show that an appropriate kinetic relaxation substantially enlarges the stable parameter domain. In a Taylor-Green convergence test with consistent initialization, all three operators converge at second order, and their error differences follow the hyperviscous coefficient for diagonal shear waves: the E-RLBM error is about 6% above the BGK error and about 40% below the RLBM error; in a double shear layer at Re = 80000, the E-RLBM follows the RLBM convergence curve. The proposed collision operator therefore provides a low-cost means of controlling nonhydrodynamic modes without introducing a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.

entry.title: Stiff source terms inside ADER-DG method
entry.summary: ADER-DG numerical method with the LST-DG predictor, when used to solve hyperbolic equations with stiff source terms, exhibits properties characteristic of IMEX computational schemes. With increasing stiffness, characterized by the parameter $z = ν{Δt}^{n} < 0$, the maximum of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}$ of the ADER-DG numerical method increases. In the region of strong stiffness $|z| \gg 1$, a linear increase in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z) \sim |z|$ occurs. In the region of small source terms $|z| \ll 1$, the results $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ transform into known results for the problem $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(0)$ without source terms. In the transition region $|z| \sim 1$, a range of insignificant decrease in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ is discovered. In the linear case, instability is violated precisely when one of the matrix eigenvalues reaches $λ= -1$, regardless of the phase $θ$ of the numerical solution. A rigorous stability theory of the ADER-DG numerical method for stiff problems for arbitrary degree $N$ of basis polynomials is constructed. The stability condition is simplified to solving a polynomial equation for the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}$. Highly accurate dependencies of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(N, z)$ of the ADER-DG method on the parameter $z$ are obtained. A rigorous direct proof of the approximation of the ADER-DG method is presented. Approximation orders $p = N+1$ for arbitrary degrees $N$ are rigorously derived. A set of numerical experiments is carried out to apply the ADER-DG method to solving both a linear advection-reaction equation and the system of Euler equations for a two-component reacting medium. The results obtained in these calculations confirm the theoretical results well.

entry.title: CARS: a centerline-anchored attention surrogate for coronary blood flow on skeleton-generated lumen geometries
entry.summary: When the parameter of a PDE surrogate is the flow domain itself, the key/value set of an attention model must encode that domain. We present CARS (Coronary Artery Rapid Surrogate), a learned surrogate for the finite-volume solution map of the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on coronary lumens built from image-derived centerlines. CARS maps a centerline with per-point lumen radius and a scalar inlet flow rate to pressure and velocity at arbitrary query points. The attention focal set is the case's own centerline, so geometry fusion costs $O(N n_f)$ rather than $O(N^2)$ in the number of evaluation points. Trained per territory on $2{,}700$ OpenFOAM solutions with synthetic focal lesions, CARS reaches relative $\ell_2$ errors of $0.120/0.149$ (pressure/velocity) on left-coronary and $0.063/0.119$ on right-coronary test sets, in $87$~ms per case against a solver wall-clock of $572$-$1{,}063$~s. It outperforms four parameter-matched neural operators, and accuracy saturates eightfold below the operating focal count. Fractional flow reserve derived from the predicted pressure matches the CFD label at Pearson $r = 0.941/0.993$ and reproduces the $\mathrm{FFR}\le 0.8$ decision in $97.7\%/96.3\%$ of held-out cases. The predicted velocity does not satisfy continuity closely enough for derived quantities, and the weights are territory-specific.

entry.title: Predicting droplet landing in angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting
entry.summary: Nozzle-free droplet generation eliminates the need for a dispensing orifice, but useful printing also requires control over where droplets are deposited. Here we demonstrate predictable droplet deposition using a nozzle-free, angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting platform. Opposing focused interdigital transducers steer droplets from a pendant parent drop toward a collection substrate, with the ejection angle set by the time-integrated acoustic acceleration imbalance. The overall acceleration ratio identifies the operating window for single-droplet ejection and separates it from no-ejection, satellite-droplet, and multiple-droplet regimes. We then connect ejection angle to landing position through a geometric deposition model referenced to a balanced shot in each experiment. At a 5.2 mm parent-drop-to-substrate spacing, 80 steered shots across twenty experiments show strongly anisotropic relative placement scatter: 0.59 mm in the steering direction and 0.06 mm transverse to it. In tests conducted independently over several days, a model calibrated on six earlier collection dates predicted landing positions on two later dates with a root-mean-square error of 0.71 mm; bootstrap resampling placed the 95% confidence range for this error between 0.41 and 1.01 mm. The results establish a practical framework for predicting relative droplet landing in angle-controlled surface acoustic wave jetting and identify the limits imposed by steering angle, separation distance, and actuation regime from an orifice-free, clog-free droplet ejection method.

entry.title: Finite time implosions of the multidimensional compressible Euler equations with a finite far-field cutoff
entry.summary: We study the problem of finite time singularities in the isentropic compressible Euler equations in multiple dimensions with radial symmetry. Our initial data consists of the radially symmetric Kidder self-similar implosion with a continuous constant density cutoff. Motivated by our recent work on the one-dimensional problem, we present high-resolution radially symmetric adaptive mesh refinement simulations that when combined with asymptotic similarity solution analysis present a full picture of the ensuing dynamics of the implosion. From the cutoff point in the initial data, an expanding wave emerges. The endpoints of the wave follow the "imploding" and "exploding" characteristic speeds associated with the system of hyperbolic conservation laws. This wave has much more complex structure than the exact non-centered rarefaction wave that emerges in the one-dimensional problem. As in the one-dimensional case, the inner Kidder solution is swallowed up by the expanding wave as time approaches the singularity time. However, unlike the one-dimensional case, a blowup occurs along the point where the `imploding' side of the expanding wave attaches to the Kidder solution. This composite blowup has an asymptotic self-similar form that has an interpretation in terms of the Gurderley-type self-similarity structure. The numerical method for the PDE necessitates a Lagrangian scheme to avoid the numerical diffusion inherent in Eulerian methods. We use a leapfrog method coupled to recursive refinement of the mesh near the blowup, which allows for very high resolution simulations, resolving many orders of magnitude of the self-similar blowup. Consistent with prior rigorous results for these equations, the blowup does not involve mass concentration and exhibits a critical $L^p$ space for the concentration of the density, depending on the dimension of space.

entry.title: Shear-induced mechanical yielding controls cluster morphology and dynamics in aggregating non-Brownian suspensions
entry.summary: In sheared aggregating suspensions, flow drives both the formation and breakage of particle clusters, whose dynamic evolution influences transport and rheological properties. Understanding these mechanisms remains challenging due to the complex interplay between interparticle forces, hydrodynamic interactions, and shear flow. Using parallelized Accelerated Stokesian Dynamics (PASD) simulations, we investigate cluster microstructure and rotational dynamics, and how their coupling produces suspension stress in sheared, attractive non-Brownian suspensions. When interparticle attraction dominates over separating shear forces, clusters grow until mechanical loading balances maximum interparticle bond strength. We examine how the cluster stresslet depends on cluster size, with both quantities normalized by their mechanical yielding scales. Scaled cluster stresslets collapse onto a master curve exhibiting three distinct regimes: cubic, quadratic, and linear with respect to the scaled radius of gyration $R_g$. In the cubic regime, small, compact clusters behave as rigid bodies, whose hydrodynamic stresslet scales with cluster volume $R_g^3$. As clusters grow into the quadratic regime, low-aspect-ratio clusters preferentially yield under flow, driving a proportional increase in average aspect ratio with size. High-aspect-ratio clusters follow Jeffery rotational dynamics within the flow-gradient plane, spending longer durations aligned with the flow and thereby reducing their time-averaged hydrodynamic stresslet to scale as $R_g^2$. In the linear regime, clusters approach the maximum size sustainable by the interparticle bonds. The internal tension is bounded by the maximum bond strength, limiting the stresslet to an $R_g$ dependence. These findings establish a mechanistic framework connecting microscale cluster morphology and dynamics to macroscale rheology.

entry.title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows
entry.summary: Matrix-product-state (MPS) and quantized tensor-train (QTT) representations offer a promising framework for computational fluid dynamics, with logarithmic run time and memory scaling in mesh size when bond dimensions remain bounded. Existing MPS-based solvers are Eulerian: they compress velocity fields and enforce immersed-body boundary conditions through static masks or body-fitted coordinates. Moving or flexible bodies complicate this approach: deformation requires updating MPS masks every time step, while filamentary vorticity in high-Reynolds-number flows may resist low-rank compression. We propose a complementary approach: compress the Biot--Savart kernel rather than the flow state, evolve vorticity using Lagrangian vortex particles, and represent immersed bodies by bound vortex sheets on Lagrangian surface points. Our main theoretical result is a lifting theorem: QTT rank $r$ of the kernel implies matrix-product-operator (MPO) rank at most $2^d r$ for the corresponding convolution operator in $d$ dimensions, independent of grid resolution. This bound is sharp for our interleaved ordering. With quantics tensor cross interpolation, the moment-to-local stage of a single-level fast multipole method becomes a precomputed tensor-network contraction with quasi-linear complexity, retaining Lagrangian flexibility for immersed bodies. Our PyTorch implementation (\texttt{DiffVortex}) is end-to-end differentiable, runs on GPUs, and handles $6.7\times10^{7}$ particles on a single device. We validate against reference vortex-method results for an impulsively started cylinder and exact and reference solutions for inviscid elliptical vortices. We also demonstrate two-dimensional flows past rigidly moving, multiple, and deforming bodies, including gradients propagated through the full time integration.

entry.title: Acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a through-hole MHz transducer
entry.summary: This experimental study demonstrates MHz-order acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a compact through-hole lithium niobate thickness-mode transducer integrated at the nozzle exit and driven near its 6.7 MHz resonance. Jet dynamics were measured by high-speed shadowgraphy at 50,000 fps, and breakup lengths were obtained from instantaneous jet-length records using an autocorrelation-based method that identifies statistically separated breakup events. Acoustic actuation produced visible interfacial corrugations and reduced the normalized breakup length, $L_b/d$, for both water and glycerol--water jets. In water, the response was threshold-like at low Weber number and weakened as the jet velocity increased to We ~ 50. A reduced-order threshold correlation, fit to the water amplitude and velocity sweeps, captured this abrupt shortening and the subsequent loss of actuation efficacy. More viscous glycerol--water mixtures shortened immediately at low forcing, indicating a distinct acoustic-coupling regime rather than a universal collapse of the water response. A wetting-control experiment showed that liquid spreading at the nozzle base can also shorten the jet, so the measured response reflects coupled radiation-pressure forcing, capillary-wave feedback, and wetting-mediated disturbance injection. Resolved droplet tracking further showed that MHz excitation changes the visible gate-crossing droplet population, although sub-resolution mist and micron-scale atomization were not measured. These results establish through-hole MHz actuation as a compact route for modifying free-surface jet breakup and provide a repeatable image-analysis protocol for experimental-fluid-mechanics measurements.

entry.title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics
entry.summary: We present Swarmlet, a GPU solver for the unsteady aerodynamics and flight dynamics of one or many multirotor vehicles. The wake is a meshless, evolving-core vortex particle field in the reformulated (rVPM) large-eddy formulation, coupled to rotor models of three fidelities, six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control. Particles carry a smooth core of compact support whose field outside four core radii is exactly the singular Biot-Savart field, so the multipole far field of the treecode carries no regularization error. The subfilter closure is a dynamic eddy viscosity on a fixed filter width, applied by core spreading with a Lagrangian exchange of its local excess under an explicit stability bound, and the strengths are relaxed by projection; global corrections make both the exchange and the relaxation conserve total vorticity and linear impulse. All rotor models shed connected bound circulation, the disks along the arcs swept in each step however long, so the wake receives the lift impulse. The solver agrees with direct summation to $5\times 10^{-7}$ and converges at third order in time. Without calibration, an actuator-line model that includes its own near sheet predicts the hover thrust of a DJI 9443 propeller within 2%. With calibrated section polars it reproduces a Crazyflie propeller's thrust and torque within 3.2% at three speeds and the near wake of a hovering quadrotor with relative $L^2$ differences of 0.08-0.21 against particle image velocimetry, while the wake keeps the delivered impulse. A closed-loop formation of 100 quadrotors, run at a coarser setting on one GPU, illustrates the coupled method at swarm scale.

entry.title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
entry.summary: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

entry.title: Hydrodynamics of microalgae in sea spray
entry.summary: Airborne transmission of biological matter is likely to cause numerous respiratory distress in coastal populations during certain harmful algal blooms. While we know that dissolved algal toxins aerosolize, the contribution of particle-associated toxins is still unknown. The observation of microalgae in the atmosphere suggests that cells or cell debris could be a carrier. Exchange of particulate matter between ocean and atmosphere is driven by sea spray: microplastics and bacteria aerosolize in jet droplets, following the bursting of air bubbles. However, current models for particle capture only consider surface effects, which fail to explain how large microalgal cells (5-50 um) can be entrapped in jet drops (100-800 um). Here, we demonstrate with a variety of species that microalgae are consistently captured in jet drops, and derive a new particle capture model based on the hydrodynamics of the jet. Using the enrichment factor, which measures the increase in concentration in the first jet drop relative to the bulk, we uncover two regimes. The transition between regimes strongly depends on cell size. In addition, we highlight the dynamics of particles within the jet and derive an enrichment model based on hydrodynamics rather than surface considerations. This work widens and generalizes established results on bacterial and microplastic entrapment in jet drops, resolving discrepancies found in the literature. Finally, we demonstrate that sea spray can aerosolize toxic Ostreopsis cf. ovata cells. This reveals a potential particulate pathway for airborne toxicity during harmful algal blooms and raises the question of the relative contribution of particles to that of dissolved toxins.

entry.title: Dynamics of liquid jet breakup and droplet size distribution in a crossflow airstream
entry.summary: The fragmentation of a liquid jet in a crossflowing airstream arises from a complex interplay between aerodynamic forcing and interfacial instabilities acting across a wide range of length scales. We examine the spatial evolution of droplet size distributions along the jet trajectory using a combination of high-speed shadowgraphy and digital in-line holography, allowing simultaneous characterization of jet morphology and volumetric droplet size distributions. The results demonstrate a clear progression of breakup mechanisms, from near-field bag rupture to downstream rim, ligament, and node disintegration, each associated with distinct characteristic length scales. This evolution is reflected in the droplet size distributions, which broaden and become increasingly polydisperse downstream relative to the near-field distributions. By systematically varying the liquid-jet and airstream Weber numbers, we identify distinct breakup modes, and construct a regime map that delineates the column-breakup, isolated-bag-breakup, and interacting-bag regimes. Furthermore, by incorporating the dominant instability mechanisms, including Rayleigh-Taylor and Rayleigh-Plateau instabilities associated with the observed column, bag, and multi-bag breakup modes, we develop a theoretical framework for jet atomization in crossflow. The framework relates instability wavelengths to characteristic droplet sizes, and reasonably captures the experimentally observed trends. We found that stronger aerodynamic forcing induces earlier breakup, decreases the characteristic instability length scales, and generates finer droplets dispersed over a wider spatial region. Overall, the study establishes a quantitative relationship between instability-driven fragmentation dynamics and droplet size distributions, thereby connecting interfacial instabilities with measurable spray characteristics.

entry.title: Computational and experimental study of multi-grain-size sediment transport and sorting process
entry.summary: Successful prediction of the interaction between turbulent flows and river ecosystems is essential for flood management, development of mitigation strategies, and infrastructure protection. Natural riverbeds consist of bed materials of multiple grain sizes that interact with turbulence differently, leading to spatial classification of particle sizes. Such particle sorting processes can only be captured by models capable of handling multiple grain sizes. We present a numerical framework that couples large-eddy simulation with a multi-grain-size sediment transport module to track multiple grain size classes, their local fractions within the bed-load layer, and bed evolution. A laboratory experiment was conducted in a flume with multi-size bed material to examine sediment particle redistribution and sorting. Measured sediment grain size distributions and bed elevations were used to validate the numerical framework. The results of the multi-grain-size sediment transport model for bed deformation were then compared against those of a uniform sediment transport model, demonstrating that the former reduces the prediction errors relative to the experimental measurements from 37.98 to 3.83 percent for maximum scour depth and from 48.35 to 11.54 percent for maximum deposition height. The validated numerical framework was also applied to large-scale meandering rivers with multi-grain bed material, simulating their bed deformation and sediment sorting. The simulation results revealed the formation of particle sorting patterns in meandering rivers, with coarser and finer sediment particles accumulating near the erosional depression (scour) and depositional (point bar) regions, respectively. These findings support the coupled framework's ability to predict sediment particle sorting and highlight the importance of representing bed material heterogeneity in numerical modeling of meandering rivers.

entry.title: Monocular 3D bubble reconstruction: DNS-informed ray tracing and deep learning
entry.summary: Bubble size, depth, and spatial distribution govern transport and uniformity in multiphase flows. A single shadowgraphic view cannot separate bubble diameter from focal-plane displacement, as image signatures depend on both, while multicamera systems add optical access, calibration, and cost. We develop a single-camera physics-guided framework combining direct numerical simulation (DNS), validated Monte Carlo ray tracing, preprocessing, and focus-conditioned multitask deep learning to recover three-dimensional bubble position and physical-equivalent diameter from two-dimensional shadowgraphs. DNS-resolved bubble label images rendered at multiple focal-plane settings. The ray tracer reproduces shadowgraphic signatures with errors below $3\%$ (intensity), $1\%$ (apparent size), $15\%$ (blur), $6\%$ (numerical aperture), and $4\%$ (edge-spread-function shape), running $\sim30\times$ faster than the CPU implementation. The dataset has $900$ frames and $87{,}728$ labeled instances, partitioned by DNS timestamp to prevent leakage and expanded to over $10^{5}$ crops by broad-depth controlled-density rendering. A multitask network predicts signed depth and diameter from crops and focal-plane coordinates, achieving $\sim97.6\%$ normalized depth accuracy on held-out data; a closed-loop DNS-to-image-to-reconstruction test of $180$ bubbles gives diameter error below $9.71\%$ ($\sim90.29\%$ accuracy). On experimental images at four radial planes ($142$--$971$ bubbles each), PDF overlap is $68\%$--$92\%$ and log-PDF correlation is $0.72$--$0.87$. At the focal reference plane ($11{,}679$ bubbles), overlap is $\sim86\%$, correlation is $0.93$, and full-distribution, $D_{99.8}$, and composite errors are below $7.7\%$, increasing with focal-plane distance and defining a recoverability limit. Without stereoscopic hardware, the framework offers a scalable diagnostic for dense bubbly flows.

entry.title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows
entry.summary: A graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder is leveraged to produce reduced latent graph representations of detonation-containing flows. In a two-dimensional hydrogen-air channel configuration with a uniform fuel-air mixture, it was found that latent graphs with effective resolutions of twice the induction length are capable of reconstructing both the wavefront and the post-shock region of the cellular detonation wave structure. Extrapolation studies using stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations revealed an intrinsic property of GNN-based reconstruction from reduced latent graphs -- a representational hierarchy, rooted in the local nature of message passing, that tends to prioritize features at the detonation front (i.e., the wavefront profile and triple points) over the downstream deflagrative regions. In particular, it was found that at a fixed ambient condition, the information contained in uniform two-dimensional detonations was sufficient to reconstruct the wavefront structure of both stratified and three-dimensional detonations. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of GNNs for both reduction and information overlap extraction in detonation-containing flows, opening promising pathways for accelerated simulations of these flows.

entry.title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
entry.summary: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

entry.title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface
entry.summary: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.
